Cloud Computing · Session spec for the design team

Deployment & Service Models

Session 2 · from 2. Deployment & Service Models.docx
55 slides174 clicks 37 beats8 TR images
A deployment model says who owns the cloud and who shares it; a service model says how much of the stack the provider runs for you. Both are choices, and cost decides between them.

How to use this page

  1. One card below is one slide, in order. The grey box is a sketch of the slide's words, not the design.
  2. Words are exact. Copy the kicker, heading, lead, points, tables and code as written. If something does not fit, ask; do not rewrite it.
  3. Clicks say what appears on each click. Click 1 is what shows when the slide opens.
  4. Draw and TR visual guidance say what the picture is. Your call is yours to design.
  5. Images: Use as-is real screenshots, crop as noted. Redraw in template colours a correct diagram to draw again. Do not use wrong or decorative.
  6. The same spec, for tools, is spec.json in this folder. There are no speaker notes in either, by design.

Overview

By the end, a student can

  • Name the four deployment models and say who owns and who shares each.
  • Tell multi-cloud from hybrid cloud, and give its three motivations and its cost.
  • Say which layers the provider manages in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, with a service for each.
  • Place FaaS, serverless and AI/ML-as-a-Service beyond SaaS, and say what the user still manages.
  • Tell CapEx from OpEx, say what TCO adds, and pick on-demand, committed use or spot for a workload.

Comes after: 1 - Cloud Computing Fundamentals
Next: Virtualization & Hypervisors

Notes for the whole deck

  • One spectrum runs through section 1: fully shared to fully dedicated (T01-2). The colour scale on T06-1 is that spectrum.
  • One stack runs through section 3: T10-1 draws it, T11-1, T12-1 and T13-1 reuse it with the owner line moving up. T14-1 and T17-1 extend the same direction past SaaS.
  • Every analogy is its own card, after the concept it explains. Familiar side first, concept side second, parts lined up.
  • Logos for AWS, Azure, GCP and every named service come from slide-kit/assets first (content rules 12 and 13).
  • Every TR image is listed in meta.tr_images. Redraw what is marked redraw in template colours; never paste it in.

Rules for every slide

Content

  • Words are exact. kicker, heading, lead, show, table, code and analogy.text are final. If one does not fit, ask for a change to the spec; do not rewrite it.
  • Nothing the TR does not say. No added facts, examples, numbers or questions.
  • No autoplay. Nothing moves on a timer. One press, one change.
  • Text and the part of the figure it describes appear on the same press.
  • Simple English. No em dashes anywhere. No full stop at the end of a line.
  • Template colours, type and chrome only (RULES.md 32 to 37). Never a colour taken from a TR image.
  • A technology named on a slide carries its logo, from slide-kit/assets first.
  • The quiz frame says Quiz Time! and nothing else.

Build

  • One self-contained HTML file built with the slide template. It opens offline and makes no network request.
  • Every card in this spec is one slide, in this order. Press 1 is what shows when the slide opens.
  • Every slide's outer element carries data-spec="<card id>" and data-presses="<press_count>".
  • Right arrow or the clicker is one press. Left arrow goes back one press.
  • Slide components come from the kit (slide-kit/slide-template/src/slides and src/ui). A new component is a kit change and needs a PR.
  • There are no speaker notes in this spec, and the deck carries none from the TR.

Cloud Deployment Models Landscape

concept · tr:slide 1
T01-1

What a deployment model decides

tr:slide 1ContentSlidePeerCards
Deployment Models Map
Four Ways To Deploy
A cloud deployment model defines who owns the infrastructure, where it is hosted, and who has access to it
  • Different organisations choose different deployment models based on their control, security, scalability, and sharing requirements

A deployment model answers three questions: who owns the infrastructure, where it is hosted, who can use it.

Clicks (2)

  1. 1
    Kicker, heading and the lead. Under it, three empty labelled slots: owns, hosted, access.
  2. 2
    The second line appears and the four needs it names (control, security, scalability, sharing) arrive as four chips on the same press.

Draw

Three slots for the three questions the lead asks, then four chips for the four needs. No cloud clip art.

Must

  • The four needs are the TR's words: control, security, scalability, sharing.

Your call

How the slots and chips look.

T01-2

The four models, on one spectrum

tr:slide 1ContentSlideRadialSpread
Deployment Models Map
Four Ways To Deploy
Let’s explore the four major deployment models
  • Public cloud: provider-owned, shared across tenants
  • Private cloud: dedicated, either on-premise or hosted
  • Hybrid cloud: private and public linked together
  • Community cloud: shared by organisations with common needs

Four deployment models sit on one line from fully shared to fully dedicated.

Clicks (5)

  1. 1
    Kicker, heading and the line Let’s explore the four major deployment models. The centre node Infrastructure Choice alone.
  2. 2
    Point 1, Public cloud: provider-owned, shared across tenants, appears as one box around the centre node, on the same press.
  3. 3
    Point 2, Private cloud: dedicated, either on-premise or hosted, appears as one box around the centre node, on the same press.
  4. 4
    Point 3, Hybrid cloud: private and public linked together, appears as one box around the centre node, on the same press.
  5. 5
    Point 4, Community cloud: shared by organisations with common needs, appears as one box around the centre node, on the same press.

TR visual guidance

Four boxes labelled Public, Private, Hybrid, Community arranged around a central 'Infrastructure Choice' node, arrows showing a spectrum from fully shared to fully dedicated

Draw

The TR guidance as drawn: four boxes around a centre node. Add the spectrum as one axis under the boxes, Public at the shared end and Private at the dedicated end, Hybrid and Community between.

Must

  • The spectrum runs from fully shared to fully dedicated, and Public and Private sit at its two ends.

Your call

Layout of the four boxes and the axis.

Public Cloud Explained

concept · tr:slide 2
T02-1

Public cloud

tr:slide 2ContentRightImageSlide
Public Cloud
Shared Multi-Tenant Infrastructure
A public cloud is a cloud environment where a cloud provider owns and manages the infrastructure, and multiple customers use its resources over the internet
  • Infrastructure owned and run entirely by the provider
  • Many tenants share hardware, isolated logically from each other
  • Capacity scales rapidly across resources pooled across customers
  • Best fit: variable workloads, fast launch, low compliance limits

In a public cloud the provider owns everything and many customers share it over the internet.

Clicks (5)

  1. 1
    Kicker, heading, lead. On the right, the provider cloud in the middle with nobody connected yet.
  2. 2
    Point 1, Infrastructure owned and run entirely by the provider, appears.
  3. 3
    Point 2, Many tenants share hardware, isolated logically from each other, appears, and Enterprise P, Enterprise Q and User R connect to the provider cloud on the same press.
  4. 4
    Point 3, Capacity scales rapidly across resources pooled across customers, appears.
  5. 5
    Point 4, Best fit: variable workloads, fast launch, low compliance limits, appears.

TR visual guidance

One large building labelled 'Provider Data Centre' with multiple small logos (different companies) drawing from it over an internet cloud icon

Draw

Redraw the TR image: one provider cloud in the centre, Enterprise P, Enterprise Q and User R each with an arrow from it. That is the TR guidance's "many tenants drawing from one provider".

Must

  • Every tenant connects to the same one provider cloud.

Your call

Hybrid Cloud And Cloud Bursting

concept · tr:slide 4
T04-1

Hybrid cloud

tr:slide 4ContentRightImageSlide
Hybrid Cloud
Cloud Bursting Explained
Hybrid cloud links private and public infrastructure so workloads move between them, avoiding the need to size on-premise capacity for rare demand peaks

Hybrid cloud links a private cloud and a public cloud so work can move between them.

Clicks (2)

  1. 1
    Kicker, heading, lead. On the right, the private side alone.
  2. 2
    The public side arrives beside it, with the link between the two drawn on the same press.

Draw

Redraw the TR image: private cloud on the left, public cloud on the right, one link between them. Use a line, not the image's plus sign: the point is that they are connected.

Your call

Icons.

T04-2

Cloud bursting

tr:slide 4ContentSlideGateFlow
Hybrid Cloud
Cloud Bursting Explained
  • Sudden overload bursts into public cloud capacity temporarily
  • Cloud bursting: automatic overflow triggered by demand thresholds
  • Example: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into on-premise sites

When load crosses a threshold, the overflow goes to the public cloud for a while, then comes back.

Clicks (4)

  1. 1

  3. 3
    Point 2, Cloud bursting: automatic overflow triggered by demand thresholds, appears; the threshold line is labelled demand threshold on the same press.
  4. 4
    Point 3, Example: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into on-premise sites, appears with the AWS logo.

TR visual guidance

Two linked boxes, 'Private Infrastructure' and 'Public Cloud', with a dashed arrow labelled 'burst' flowing from private to public only when a load gauge crosses a threshold line

Must

  • The burst arrow appears only once the gauge is past the threshold line.
  • Bursting is temporary: nothing on the card suggests the workload moves for good.

Must not

  • Animate the gauge on a timer.

Your call

The gauge and the arrow.

Community Cloud Explained

concept · tr:slide 5
T05-1

Community cloud

tr:slide 5ContentRightImageSlide
Community Cloud
Shared Among Peers
Community cloud is infrastructure shared by several organisations with common regulatory, security or mission needs, rather than opened to the general public
  • Governance and compliance rules set jointly by member organisations
  • Cost split among fewer tenants than public, more than solo private
  • Example: AWS GovCloud (US), reserved for government agencies and partners
  • Typical users: government bodies, healthcare consortiums, research collaborations

A community cloud is shared by a group of organisations with the same needs, and closed to everyone else.

  5. 5
    Point 4, Typical users: government bodies, healthcare consortiums, research collaborations, appears, and the government, healthcare and research icons connect to the block on the same press.

Multi-Cloud: Beyond Hybrid

concept · tr:slide 7
T07-1

Multi-cloud

tr:slide 7ContentSlideFanOut
Multi-Cloud Defined
Multiple Providers Together
Multi-cloud means running workloads across two or more independent public providers at once, unlike hybrid cloud, which mixes public with private infrastructure
  • AWS handles general-purpose compute and storage workloads
  • Azure serves Microsoft-integrated enterprise applications
  • GCP powers data analytics and AI/ML pipelines

Multi-cloud uses two or more public providers at the same time, which is not the same as hybrid.

  4. 4
    Point 3, GCP powers data analytics and AI/ML pipelines, appears; the arrow to that provider's logo, labelled with its workload, appears on the same press.

Why Organizations Adopt Multi-Cloud

concept · tr:slide 8
T08-1

Why multi-cloud

tr:slide 8ContentSlidePeerCards
Multi-Cloud Motivations
Resilience Negotiation Regulation
Three business pressures push organizations toward multiple providers even though it adds complexity
  • Resilience: a second provider keeps services running during an outage
  • Negotiation leverage: comparing quotes across vendors avoids one-sided pricing
  • Regulation: in-country hosting or concentration-risk rules may require a compliant region or a second provider

Three pressures push a company to more than one provider: resilience, negotiation and regulation.

Cost Of Multi-Cloud Complexity

What multi-cloud costs to run

tr:slide 9ContentSlideDataTable
Operational Overhead Cost
Managing Multiple Platforms
Multi-cloud earns its resilience and leverage at a real operational price: every added provider multiplies what must be learned, managed and paid for
  • Separate consoles, APIs and billing dashboards per provider
  • Distinct certifications and skill sets needed for each platform's staff
  • Cross-cloud data transfer (egress) charges between providers
  • Duplicate monitoring, security and IAM policies to maintain

Each provider added repeats the skills, tools, billing and security work.

Beyond IaaS, PaaS And SaaS

concept · tr:slide 14
T14-1

Beyond the big three

tr:slide 14ContentSlideSpineFlow
Beyond The Big Three
New Service Models
Cloud service models did not stop at IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Two further models push abstraction higher, changing what the provider manages and what the developer retains
  • Function as a Service (FaaS): runs code per trigger, no visible server
  • Serverless: broader term covering FaaS plus managed databases and queues
  • AI/ML-as-a-Service: consumes pre-built AI and ML models via API
  • Both shift most infrastructure responsibility onto the cloud provider

FaaS, serverless and AI/ML-as-a-Service go further than SaaS: the provider takes on more, the user keeps less.

Function As A Service And Serverless

concept · tr:slide 15
T15-1

FaaS and serverless

tr:slide 15ContentSlideSpineFlow
FaaS And Serverless
Pay Per Execution
Function as a Service (FaaS) runs a single function only when triggered, removing any need to provision or manage a server
  • Triggers: HTTP request, scheduled timer, queue message, file upload
  • Scales automatically from zero to many parallel invocations
  • Billed per invocation and execution time, not idle time
  • Runs on AWS Lambda; cold start delay if idle first

A function runs only when something triggers it, and is billed only for that run.

  4. 4
    Point 3, Billed per invocation and execution time, not idle time, appears, and torn down is added: the timeline is back to idle.
  5. 5
    Point 4, Runs on AWS Lambda; cold start delay if idle first, appears, and the AWS Lambda logo labels the timeline.

CapEx vs OpEx: The Accounting View

concept · tr:slide 19
T19-1

CapEx and OpEx

tr:slide 19ContentSlideSplitCompare
CapEx vs OpEx
Balance Sheet Impact
Cloud does not just change how much is paid; it changes which financial statement absorbs the cost, reshaping approvals and tax treatment
  • CapEx: capitalised, depreciated over asset life, sits on balance sheet
  • OpEx: expensed immediately, hits the income statement same period

CapEx goes on the balance sheet and is spread over years; OpEx is an expense in the same period.

Clicks (3)

    Kicker, heading, lead. The split panel's two headings: Balance sheet, Income statement.

tr:slide 19ContentSlideDataTable
CapEx vs OpEx
Balance Sheet Impact
  • CapEx typically needs board-level capital approval
  • OpEx approval sits within departmental budgets
  • Depreciation deductions (CapEx) shift tax timing versus OpEx's immediate deduction
  • AWS Cost and Usage Report classifies spend for finance systems

The two kinds of spend are approved by different people and taxed at different times.

Total Cost of Ownership Defined

concept · tr:slide 20
T20-1

What TCO adds up

tr:slide 20ContentSlideLayerAnatomy
Total Cost Ownership
Beyond The Price Tag
Total cost of ownership (TCO) totals every direct and indirect cost of running a workload across its life, not only the sticker price
  • Direct costs: compute, storage, licensing, network transfer
  • Indirect costs: staffing, training, downtime, migration effort
  • On-premise adds power, cooling, floor space, hardware refresh

TCO is every cost of a workload over its life, and the price tag is only the bottom layer.

Pricing Models: On-Demand, Committed & Spot

concept · tr:slide 21
T21-1

Three pricing models

tr:slide 21ContentSlidePeerCards
Three Pricing Models
On-Demand To Spot
Providers meter usage but let buyers trade commitment for discount; three payment patterns cover most cloud spend
  • On-demand: metered pay-as-used rate, zero commitment
  • Committed use: one to three-year term for lower fixed rate
  • Spot: spare capacity at a steep discount; can be reclaimed at short notice
  • Trade-off across all three: flexibility versus price

Buyers trade commitment for a lower price: on-demand, committed use, spot.

Pricing models compared

tr:slide 22ContentSlideDataTable
Pricing Models Compared
Discount And Risk
Each pricing model suits a different workload shape; committed-use discounts deepen with longer terms and more upfront payment
ModelCommitmentTypical DiscountKey RiskBest For
On-DemandNoneBaseline rateHighest unit price; cost runs on if left runningUnpredictable, short-lived workloads
Committed Use1 or 3 yearsUp to ~70% off on-demandUpfront lock-in, must forecast usageSteady, predictable baseline load
SpotNoneUp to ~90% off on-demandReclaimed with short notice (~2 min AWS, ~30 sec Azure/GCP)Fault-tolerant batch, stateless jobs

Each pricing model fits a different shape of workload.

Indian Cloud Providers & Data Residency

concept · tr:slide 24
T24-1

Indian providers

tr:slide 24ContentRightImageSlide
Indian Cloud Providers
Regional Alternatives
Alongside global hyperscalers, Indian providers compete on data residency, latency for local users, and rupee-denominated billing
  • CtrlS, Yotta, E2E Networks: private data-centre players
  • Government's GI Cloud (MeghRaj) hosts public-sector workloads
  • BFSI and government workloads often mandate in-country storage
  • Regional providers can undercut hyperscaler pricing for local traffic

Indian providers compete on data kept in India, low latency for local users, and billing in rupees.
